analysis.one_liner: Designates about 924,000 acres of Oregon's Owyhee canyonlands as wilderness while locking in livestock grazing across Malheur County.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced on December 17, 2025 with no cosponsors and referred to the House Natural Resources Committee; no hearing or vote has been scheduled.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would put roughly 924,440 acres of federal land in Malheur County, Oregon — the Owyhee canyon country — into the National Wilderness Preservation System, with two smaller special management areas alongside [S2]. It would also hand the Burns Paiute Tribe a large land holding in trust and create a local committee to run restoration projects [S2]. At the same time, it binds the government's hands on grazing: livestock grazing would continue inside the new wilderness, permit holders would get to adjust their grazing with only written notice and no environmental review, and the land agency would be barred from reducing grazing on much of the rest of the county [S2]. The bill has one sponsor, no cosponsors, and has gone no further than a committee referral [S3][S4].
analysis.who_benefits: Visitors who hike, hunt, fish, or raft the Owyhee get permanent protection for the scenery and wildlife habitat there. The Burns Paiute Tribe gains roughly 21,500 acres of federal land plus its adjacent ranch into trust, and co-stewardship of the Castle Rock area [S2]. Ranchers holding grazing permits across the county also benefit: they keep every existing permit, gain the right to shift grazing seasons and water sources with two business days' written notice and no environmental review, and are protected against any reduction of grazing on lands the plan had flagged for wilderness characteristics [S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Owyhee visitors, the Burns Paiute Tribe, and grazing permit holders

how_it_helps.text: The bill designates about 924,440 acres of Malheur County federal land as wilderness in 22 named units, plus two special management areas totaling roughly 40,874 acres [S2].
The designated lands are withdrawn from new mining claims and from mineral and geothermal leasing, and from sale or other disposal under the public land laws [S2].

The Secretary of the Interior must take about 21,548 acres of federal land and 6,686 acres of the Tribe's own ranch land (Jonesboro Ranch) into trust for the Burns Paiute Tribe, plus about 2,500 acres in the Castle Rock Wilderness Study Area, and negotiate a co-stewardship agreement over a wider Castle Rock area [S2].

Grazing permit holders may, on request, adjust grazing seasons, pasture rotation dates, and water sources by up to 14 days with written notice two business days in advance; the variance takes effect immediately, is final agency action, and requires no review under the National Environmental Policy Act [S2].

The bill establishes a local 'Malheur C.E.O. Group' — including tribal representatives and grazing permit holders — to propose and fund restoration, invasive-species, and recreation projects, with federal cost-sharing of up to 75 percent [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Motorized recreationists lose open cross-country use inside the new wilderness (though the bill preserves many named road corridors). Mining and geothermal companies can no longer stake claims or lease on the designated land. The Bureau of Land Management loses management flexibility: it cannot reduce grazing on lands flagged for wilderness characteristics in its own 2024 land plan, wilderness boundaries must be trimmed back to existing grazing allotment lines, and heavy equipment use is allowed inside wilderness for livestock work [S2]. The public also keeps subsidizing grazing on the designated and nearby land, since the bill guarantees existing permits continue at their current animal-unit levels [S2].
analysis.who_pays_short: Motorized users, mining claimants, and BLM's flexibility

drawbacks.text: The bill says the Secretary 'shall not reduce or restrict grazing' for permit holders on federal land marked 'Unit Protected for Wilderness Characteristics' or 'Unit Managed for Other Resources' in the Bureau's 2024 Southeastern Oregon plan, and carries that ban forward into future land plans — permanently limiting the agency's ability to adjust grazing for rangeland health [S2].

Grazing variances are 'immediately effective upon issue,' are themselves final agency action, and 'shall not require conformance' to the grazing appeal regulations or the National Environmental Policy Act — so there is no environmental analysis or public appeal before a change takes effect [S2].
Every wilderness and special management area boundary must be adjusted so no grazing allotment is even partially included, diminishing each protected area to existing allotment lines [S2].

Congress declares that all other federal land in the county has been 'adequately inventoried and studied' for wilderness purposes and releases it from further wilderness consideration, to be managed for 'principal or major uses' — foreclosing future protection for the rest of the Owyhee country in Malheur County [S2].

The wilderness management language expressly allows chainsaws, backhoes, and tractors inside wilderness for livestock management work including doctoring cattle, distributing salt, and maintaining fences and water facilities — a broader carve-out than typical wilderness law allows [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protection side is real and permanent: nearly a million acres of intact canyon country would be shielded from mining, leasing, and disposal, and the Burns Paiute Tribe would get a substantial land base. The cost is that the bill hard-codes the grazing status quo for decades — no environmental review for grazing changes, no reduction of grazing on lands the agency itself identified as having wilderness values, and protected-area boundaries cut around every allotment. A supporter who cares most about locking in protection before development pressure arrives could reasonably accept that trade; someone focused on restoring degraded rangeland would see the bill as tying the land manager's hands at exactly the moment restoration needs flexibility. The package is a genuine bargain between conservation and grazing interests, not a one-sided giveaway — but the grazing side of the bargain is unusually binding.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in mid-December 2025 and referred to the House Natural Resources Committee, where it has sat with no hearing, no markup, and no vote scheduled.

narrative.text: Representative Cliff Bentz of Oregon introduced H.R. 6777 on December 17, 2025 [S1].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources — its only action to date [S4].
No member has cosponsored the bill [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one yet. The bill sits in committee, so the wilderness designations, tribal land transfer, and grazing lock-ins all remain on paper; current management of the Owyhee lands continues under the Bureau's existing 2024 plan.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: So far, no one — current land management continues

for.name: Owyhee wilderness conservation advocates

for.what_they_did: Long-running public campaign to designate the Owyhee canyonlands as wilderness, which bills like this respond to

sides.party_line_note: No opposition has been recorded and no votes have occurred; the only floor-level facts are that a Republican sponsor introduced the bill alone with zero cosponsors of either party [S3].

industries.industry: Livestock grazing permit holders on Malheur County public land
industries.note: The bill locks in every existing grazing permit across the county, bars the Bureau from reducing grazing on lands it had flagged for wilderness values, and lets permit holders shift seasons and water sources with two days' notice and no environmental review — a permanent, subsidized role on the public range. The counterweight is mandatory cooperative monitoring plans and annual reporting the Secretary must use to adjust management [S2].

The new wilderness areas, special management areas, and tribal trust lands are all withdrawn from new mining claims and from mineral and geothermal leasing, closing off future extraction on roughly a million acres [S2].

industries.industry: Outdoor recreation and Owyhee-area tourism businesses
industries.note: Permanent wilderness protection preserves hunting, fishing, hiking, and rafting values that draw visitors to southeast Oregon; the bill also requires the local C.E.O. Group to prioritize habitat and ecosystem restoration projects [S2].

The Tribe receives about 21,500 acres of federal land plus its ranch into trust, roughly 2,500 more acres held in trust at Castle Rock, and a formal co-stewardship agreement — while existing grazing on those lands continues unless the Tribe buys out the permits at market value [S2].

industries.industry: Motorized recreation and off-highway vehicle users
industries.note: Cross-country motorized use ends inside the new wilderness, but the bill preserves named cherry-stem and pipeline roads, keeps adjacent roads open, and allows motorized equipment in wilderness for livestock and fire work — a narrower loss than standard wilderness designation [S2].

analysis.trajectory: At two weeks old with no cosponsors, the bill's realistic path runs through the Natural Resources Committee, which handles most public-lands bills and typically requires a hearing and a markup before any floor vote. Large wilderness packages almost always need a Senate companion and a negotiated coalition of ranching, tribal, and conservation interests; this one has the negotiated structure but no demonstrated support yet. It could gain cosponsors and be folded into a broader public-lands package later in the 119th Congress; more likely at this stage it sits until it attracts bipartisan backing or expires at the end of the Congress in January 2027.
